Question 88. Extend two polynomial vectors to a basis

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 24 p. 2

Extend 1+x and 1-x to a basis of real P2.

Read the complete derivation, verification and examination decision

A zero combination gives constant coefficient a+b=0 and linear coefficient a-b=0, forcing a=b=0. They are independent and span all degree-at-most-one polynomials because half their sum is one and half their difference is x. Add x2, which is outside that span. Coefficient comparison now proves independence of all three, and the standard monomials are in their span. Thus the enlarged list is a basis. In characteristic two the original pair coincides and this extension argument changes.

Find the coordinates of a general polynomial. Write a+bx+cx2=α(1+x)+β(1-x)+γx2. Comparing coefficients gives α+β=a, α-β=b, and γ=c, hence α=(a+b)/2, β=(a-b)/2, γ=c. These unique coordinates prove both spanning and independence at once. In characteristic two, 1-x=1+x, so the first pair is dependent; adding one vector cannot remove an existing dependence. The real-field qualification justifies the divisions by two and the original basis-extension argument.

Question 89. Linearity before applying rank–nullity

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 24 p. 3

Decide which real maps are linear: x↦2x, x↦x+1, and the determinant map on 2×2 matrices.

Read the complete derivation, verification and examination decision

The scaling map preserves sums and scalar multiples, so it is linear. The shifted map sends zero to one and is not linear. Determinant is not linear: det(2I2)=4 while 2det(I2)=2. Rank–nullity applies only to the linear map in this list. The written course lists the scaling map under nonexamples, a transcription slip corrected by the definition.

Use a complete linearity check when the zero test passes. Scaling satisfies 2(αx+βy)=α(2x)+β(2y) for all scalars, so it is linear. The determinant map sends zero to zero, but that necessary condition is insufficient: homogeneity fails on 2I2 as shown. Additivity also fails because detI2+detI2=2 while det(2I2)=4. Its multiplicativity under matrix products is a different property. A rank–nullity calculation for the determinant as a linear functional would therefore be invalid; its zero set of singular matrices is not a vector subspace.

Question 90. Oxford row-space membership with a linear certificate

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Course-derived: Oxford M1, Example 121, printed pp. 42–43

For rows (1,2,-1,0), (2,1,0,3) and (0,1,1,1), determine when x=(x1,x2,x3,x4) lies in their span.

Read the complete derivation, verification and examination decision

Exact reduction gives row basis (1,0,0,8/5), (0,1,0,-1/5) and (0,0,1,6/5). Thus a combination with first three coordinates x1,x2,x3 has fourth coordinate (8x1-x2+6x3)/5. Membership is exactly 8x1+6x3=x2+5x4. This condition is sufficient as well as necessary because the three pivot coordinates freely determine the combination. It is the single annihilator restriction supplied by the right kernel for this three-dimensional row space in four coordinates.

Use the right kernel for this row-space test. Let A be the three-by-four matrix of the stated rows and put z=(-8,1,-6,5)T. Direct multiplication gives Az=0. Its rank is three, so its right kernel is exactly the line spanned by z. Every row-space vector x satisfies xz=0, giving -8x1+x2-6x3+5x4=0. Conversely that hyperplane has dimension three and contains the three-dimensional row space, so they coincide. This is a right-kernel annihilator of rows, not the left kernel of A; the left kernel is zero because all three rows are independent. Confusing the two spaces would predict the wrong ambient coordinate count.

Complete summary and examination rules

Summary: rank counts independent restrictions and attainable directions

A matrix with m rows, n columns and r pivots has an image of dimension r, a row space of dimension r, a kernel of dimension n-r and a left kernel of dimension m-r. A compatible load has a complete affine family of solutions with direction space equal to the kernel. Full column rank gives uniqueness on the image; full row rank gives existence for every load; both coincide with invertibility only for square matrices.

A complete rank-and-fiber examination decision sequence

Begin with the field and the shape A∈Fm×n. Record two different coordinate spaces: the input has dimension n and the output has dimension m. If a load is present, keep it separate from coefficient columns throughout reduction. A pivot in an augmented load column certifies inconsistency; it is not another solved input coordinate.

Next certify the rank with matching lower and upper bounds. An explicit independent column list or a nonzero minor proves a lower bound. A complete echelon reduction, a spanning dependency description, or vanishing of all larger minors proves an upper bound. One zero minor, many visible nonzero entries or the number of original equations alone cannot supply the complete certificate. For parameter families, retain branches where candidate pivots vanish before dividing.

Once r is known, compute right nullity n-r and left nullity m-r separately. Extract an image basis from the original pivot columns, a row-space basis from nonzero reduced rows, and a right-kernel basis from independent free-coordinate patterns. Check matrix annihilation, independence and the expected number of basis vectors. A zero-dimensional space has an empty basis.

For an actual load, test b∈ColA, equivalently coefficient/augmented rank equality. Over the reals, the left-kernel test YTb=0 supplies explicit independent compatibility equations. If the test fails, stop: there is no fiber to parameterize. If it succeeds, construct one particular input and add every kernel direction. Substitute the resulting formula into the original equations, not only the reduced coefficients. Report both a load criterion and a full input family whenever the question requests all solutions.

Finally interpret the result. Full column rank means uniqueness for compatible loads and existence of a left inverse. Full row rank means existence for every load and existence of a right inverse. Only finite equal dimensions identify those two conditions. For a composition, restrict the next map to the actually reached intermediate image. For a sum, keep track of shared input coordinates as well as output subspaces. For constraints on matrices or polynomials, build the linear constraint map before subtracting dimensions.

Rule 1

State the field before reducing a matrix. A coefficient that is nonzero over the reals may vanish in positive characteristic, changing both rank and nullity.

Rule 2

Record the input and output dimensions before applying rank–nullity. For an m×n matrix, input vectors have n entries and outputs have m entries.

Rule 3

Define rank as image dimension or independent pivot count. Nonzero entries and nonzero original rows are not independent restrictions.

Rule 4

A rank-zero matrix is the zero matrix. Its image and row space have empty bases, while its kernel and left kernel are full coordinate spaces.

Rule 5

The zero vector cannot occur in an independent basis list. The zero space nevertheless has dimension zero because its correct basis is the empty list.

Rule 6

A column-space basis contains m -entry vectors. A row-space basis and kernel basis contain n -entry vectors; mixing these shapes is an immediate error.

Rule 7

Row reduction preserves the kernel exactly because the left transformation is invertible. Every old zero-output input remains a zero-output input and conversely.

Rule 8

Row reduction preserves the row space exactly. Both the forward operations and their inverses express new rows in terms of old rows.

Rule 9

Row reduction generally moves the column space by an invertible output-coordinate map. Its dimension is preserved even when its position changes.

Rule 10

Find pivot indices in the reduced matrix, then select those columns from the original matrix for an original column-space basis.

Rule 11

The nonzero rows of an echelon matrix form a row-space basis. Their leading positions prove independence and their row equivalence proves spanning.

Rule 12

A zero early column can be free even when later columns contain pivots. Free coordinates are not necessarily the last consecutive coordinates.

Rule 13

A kernel basis obtained from free variables must have one independent free-coordinate pattern per direction. Verify annihilation, independence and spanning.

Rule 14

The number of kernel basis vectors equals n-r. This counts independent parameters, not the number of visible zero rows.

Rule 15

The number of left-kernel basis vectors equals m-r. Reduce the transpose or track exact row combinations to find them.

Rule 16

Row rank equals column rank over every field. The proof uses invertible reduction and standard pivot columns, not Euclidean geometry.

Rule 17

Rank is unchanged by transposition. Kernel dimensions of a rectangular matrix and its transpose can nevertheless differ.

Rule 18

Rank never exceeds the smaller matrix dimension. Any proposed dimension data must satisfy this bound before computation proceeds.

Rule 19

Full column rank means all columns are independent. It requires at least as many output coordinates as input coordinates.

Rule 20

Full row rank means all rows are independent and every output is attainable. It requires at least as many input coordinates as output coordinates.

Rule 21

A diagonal matrix's rank is its nonzero diagonal count. A general triangular matrix with zero diagonal entries can still have off-diagonal pivots.

Rule 22

Independent vectors cannot outnumber the dimension of their ambient space. A spanning list cannot contain fewer vectors than that dimension.

Rule 23

A finite independent list can be extended to a basis. A finite spanning list can be shortened to a basis by removing dependencies.

Rule 24

A singleton nonzero vector spans a one-dimensional space. Two nonzero proportional vectors still span only one dimension.

Rule 25

A homogeneous system always has the zero solution. Positive nullity describes additional directions, not inconsistency.

Rule 26

A nonhomogeneous system is compatible exactly when its load lies in the column space. Equation count alone cannot determine compatibility.

Rule 27

Appending one load column increases rank by zero or one. An increase of one proves incompatibility for that load.

Rule 28

Appending several load columns may increase rank by more than one. Equality of augmented and coefficient ranks is required for every load column to be compatible.

Rule 29

One particular solution plus every kernel direction gives all solutions. Conversely subtracting any two solutions gives a kernel vector.

Rule 30

A nonempty fiber has affine dimension n-r. It is a linear subspace only when the load is zero.

Rule 31

Fibers for different outputs are disjoint. Their common kernel direction space can make them parallel affine sets.

Rule 32

Uniqueness for one compatible load implies a zero kernel. It then implies uniqueness for every compatible load, but does not establish surjectivity.

Rule 33

Existence for one load says little about other loads. Existence for every load is the full-row-rank assertion.

Rule 34

Over an infinite field, positive nullity gives infinitely many compatible solutions. Over a finite field of q elements the count is exactly qn-r, through a bijection with the independent kernel coordinates. A field of order nine is not the non-field ring of integers modulo nine.

Rule 35

A real load b is in the column space exactly when it is orthogonal to every left-kernel vector. Testing an independent left-kernel basis gives every required output restriction. In contrast, row-space membership is tested against the right kernel in the input-coordinate space.

Rule 36

A nonzero left-kernel load pairing is an inconsistency certificate. It refutes every possible input without guessing an input.

Rule 37

For real matrices, the row space and kernel are orthogonal complements. The column space and left kernel are orthogonal complements in the output space.

Rule 38

For complex Euclidean geometry, use conjugate transpose. Plain transpose can produce a zero Gram product from a nonzero matrix.

Rule 39

Gram rank equality over the reals follows from positivity of the squared norm. Do not apply that proof over an arbitrary field.

Rule 40

Injectivity is equivalent to a zero kernel and full column rank. It means distinguishable inputs, rather than coverage of every output.

Rule 41

Surjectivity is equivalent to full row rank. It means coverage of every output, rather than uniqueness of the producing input.

Rule 42

A left inverse exists exactly for an injective finite-dimensional matrix map. Its product with the matrix is an identity on the input coordinates.

Rule 43

A right inverse exists exactly for a surjective matrix map. Its product in the opposite order is an identity on the output coordinates.

Rule 44

A tall full-column-rank real matrix has left inverse (ATA)-1AT. This construction is legal because its Gram matrix is positive definite.

Rule 45

A wide full-row-rank real matrix has right inverse AT(AAT)-1. This gives one choice among an affine family of preimages.

Rule 46

Correcting a left inverse requires correction rows in the left kernel. Correcting a right inverse requires correction columns in the kernel.

Rule 47

One-sided inverses are generally nonunique for genuinely rectangular maps. Their affine family dimensions follow by counting independent correction coordinates.

Rule 48

Square finite-dimensional injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent. This equivalence, rather than matrix shape alone, makes a one-sided inverse two-sided.

Rule 49

Infinite-dimensional shifts demonstrate that the square finite-dimensional theorem has genuine hypotheses. An onto map there can have a nonzero kernel.

Rule 50

A positive uniform lower norm bound forces injectivity. A finite square map is consequently invertible with inverse norm at most the reciprocal bound, using the same induced norm. It does not imply positive definiteness; negative identity is an explicit counterexample. Complex eigenvalues need a justified complex extension of the real norm argument.

Rule 51

A rank factorization uses original independent columns and their coordinate rows. Multiplication should reproduce every original column.

Rule 52

Rank is the smallest possible exact factorization bottleneck dimension. A product through fewer than r coordinates cannot have rank r.

Rule 53

Different full-rank factorizations differ by an invertible internal basis change. This changes intermediate coordinates while preserving the product.

Rule 54

Invertible factors on either side preserve rank. They need not preserve the literal image or kernel subspace in the original coordinates.

Rule 55

Independent domain and codomain basis changes can produce an identity-and-zero rank form. This matrix equivalence is not the same as similarity.

Rule 56

Composition rank equals the first attained image dimension minus the directions killed by the next map. Identify the actual intermediate intersection.

Rule 57

The rank of a product cannot exceed either factor's rank. A small intermediate dimension is an additional bottleneck.

Rule 58

Sylvester's lower bound uses the shared intermediate dimension n:

rank(AB)≥rankA+rankB-n

.

Rule 59

Combine a negative Sylvester expression with the independent lower bound zero. Equality with the nonnegative formal expression requires the entire kernel of A to lie in the image of B. Equality of product rank with zero instead requires the image of B to lie in the kernel of A; these are different containments.

Rule 60

If AB=0, the image of B lies in the kernel of A. A compatible dimension inequality alone does not prove that containment.

Rule 61

Product rank equals the rank of B exactly when A is injective on the image of B. This is a restriction, not necessarily global injectivity.

Rule 62

Sum rank has an upper bound by the sum of ranks and a lower bound by their absolute difference. Complete cancellation can attain zero.

Rule 63

Disjoint images alone do not force additive rank of a sum. Shared input coordinates can still restrict the number of independently controllable directions.

Rule 64

Concatenation images are sums of images. Vertical-stack kernels are intersections of kernels; the two constructions have different meanings.

Rule 65

Use the dimension formula to subtract shared directions once. Repeatedly counting an intersection overstates the size of a subspace sum.

Rule 66

Frobenius' inequality compares restrictions on nested intermediate images. Confirm all product shapes before inserting rank numbers.

Rule 67

A nonzero minor proves a lower bound on rank. One vanished minor does not prove an upper bound.

Rule 68

Rank at most r requires every minor of order r plus one to vanish. Structural column dependencies can establish the same upper bound more efficiently.

Rule 69

Separate parameter-zero branches before division. A generic RREF formula can lose exactly the exceptional cases an examination asks about.

Rule 70

At an exceptional parameter, recheck load compatibility as well as coefficient rank. A lower rank can mean either a larger fiber or no fiber.

Rule 71

Exact rank can jump from three to one at a single parameter value. Continuous entries do not force intermediate rank two to occur.

Rule 72

Constant-off-diagonal matrices can be analyzed on the all-ones line and the zero-sum space. Count the nonzero scalar actions with their correct multiplicities.

Rule 73

Exact and numerical rank answer different questions. State the numerical threshold, whether its comparison is strict, and whether it is absolute or relative to a matrix scale. Rounding a nonzero coefficient to zero changes the exact matrix; it does not prove that the original exact matrix has lower rank.

Rule 74

Block diagonal ranks add because their images occupy disjoint coordinate blocks. Block triangular matrices with singular diagonal blocks need not obey that formula.

Rule 75

A Schur-complement rank formula requires an invertible leading block. Reversible block operations justify the formula and its branch conditions.

Rule 76

A nonzero outer product has rank one. Adding it changes rank by at most one, by applying the sum bound in both directions.

Rule 77

For invertible A, a rank-one update is singular exactly when 1+vTA-1u=0. In that case its kernel is one-dimensional and its rank falls by exactly one.

Rule 78

An idempotent map splits its space into image and kernel. Rank equals trace over the reals, but orthogonality requires an additional symmetry condition.

Rule 79

A square-zero map has image contained in kernel, so rank is at most half the dimension rounded down. Nested kernels of powers stabilize permanently after their first equality.

Rule 80

Subtract the rank of independent linear constraints from the number of ambient coordinates. Prove the constraint rank with witnesses, reduction or a full parameterization. Repeated evaluations do not impose derivative conditions, repeated trace equations do not add independence, and nonlinear inequalities are not kernels of linear constraint maps.

Exact laboratory

Enter a coefficient matrix, not an augmented system. The laboratory distinguishes the four ambient spaces and returns original pivot columns, reduced nonzero rows, a kernel basis and a left-kernel basis. Every calculation uses rational arithmetic. It checks the annihilation products and rank–nullity identities; these checks certify the entered matrix only.

Accepts one to five rows and one to five columns of equal length. Use integers or exact fractions with numerator and denominator magnitude at most 100,000 and nonzero denominators. This is a coefficient matrix: no final load column is assumed. All arithmetic uses exact integer fractions.
